Consonant ⟨ν⟩ affixed to vowel endings of some Ancient Greek grammatical forms to produce euphony: in prevocalic position, to avoid sounding two vowels in a row (hiatus), and prevent elision or fusion of vowels contracting into one sound (crasis). In preconsonantal coda position, ⟨ν⟩ may be added to create a long syllable in poetic meter. Nu is also usually written before a pause at the end of a clause in prose or the end of a verse in poetry.

Paragogic nu ⟨ν⟩ (n), understood as an allomorph of certain Greek morphemic forms otherwise terminating in vowels ⟨ε⟩ (e) or ⟨ι⟩ (i), viz. third person verb and third declension dative plural noun forms, phonemically represented as -ε(ν) (-e(n)) and -ῐ(ν) (-ĭ(n)). An early Attic–Ionic innovation, nu paragoge spread through the Hellenic world; inclusion or omission of ⟨ν⟩ in ancient inscriptions is so variable and unpredictable as to suggest morphemes with and without ⟨ν⟩ occurred in free variation, not bound to the prescriptive rules of phonetic harmony codified by later Byzantine grammarians.

d.x: It is the second category which I christen, for want of a better word, epitext and which will be the subject of the last two chapters.

d.x: The benthic microflora of marine sands includes bacteria, blue-green bacteria (cyanobacteria), autotrophic flagellates, and diatoms. Those attached to sand grains are generally known as epipsammon (Fig. 4.1).

d.g: The community of biota or fauna that live on top of sand.
d.x: These groups are 1) the epipsammon, or surface-dwelling, generally motile macrofauna; 2) the endopsammon, or burrowing species that are too large to live in interstitial spaces; and 3) the mesopsammon, or interstitial fauna. The epipsammon is limited to a few groups such as fish or birds which are strong or speedy enough to exploit this turbulent environment.

d.g: Located above the cotyledons.
d.x: The basipetally differentiating epicotylar vasculature and the root-hypocotyl-cotyledon vasculature are ontogenetically separate and establish connection just below the cotyledons.

d.x: I call this epochism because it exalts one's own epoch to the contempt of other epochs. Epochism is a kind of unwisdom. Its opposite is a sense of tradition, an openness to the values that guided the lives of those before us.

epitherapeia.e: From Ancient Greek ἐπιθεραπεία (epitherapeía, “additional remedy”), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + θεραπεία (therapeía, “medical attendance, healing”).

d.g: A type of zeugma in which a single verb governs two or more clauses or phrases, placed either at the very beginning or the very end of the sentence.

epizeugma.e: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐπίζευγμα (epízeugma), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + ζεῦγμα (zeûgma, “yoke, bond”).

d.g: Without an episode.

d.g: The aggregation of conspecific insect larvae over the midvein or another elongated aspect of a leaf for coordinated defense, or to maximize feeding efficiency.
